summary: An overview of a 2002 workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board on network management, in Reston, Virginia. The workshop continued a dialog between network operators and protocol developers and was meant to guide future management work in the IETF. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3535 reports on an Internet Architecture Board workshop about network management. It records what operators needed, how participants viewed existing tools, and what work they recommended to the IETF.

subtitle: The IAB's account of operators' network-management needs and its recommendations to the IETF.

tldr.problem: Network operators told protocol developers that existing management work, especially configuration management, did not meet their needs.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a workshop, discussed six management technologies, recorded operator requirements and concerns about SNMP, and made recommendations to the IETF.
tldr.outcome: The workshop recommended focusing on configuration management and XML-based configuration work. This RFC records the workshop's discussions and recommendations; it does not define a protocol.

today: RFC 3535 is an Informational RFC published in May 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it records a workshop's views and recommendations from 2002.

sections.title: Purpose of the Workshop
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board held an invitational network-management workshop at CNRI in Reston, Virginia, from June 4 through June 6, 2002. It continued discussions between network operators and protocol developers that had taken place at earlier meetings.

Operators had said that IETF work did not address their needs, especially for configuration management. The workshop aimed to guide future IETF work by discussing technologies, operator requirements, and the SNMP framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators said that network-management tools did not meet their needs, especially when changing device settings. The IAB held a workshop to discuss those needs with protocol developers.

sections.title: Management Technologies Discussed
sections.content:
The workshop compared SNMP with MIBs, COPS-PR with PIBs, the Common Information Model (CIM), command-line interfaces accessed through TELNET or SSH, HTTP and HTML, and XML. The report lists advantages and disadvantages for each rather than choosing one technology for every task.

For example, participants said SNMP worked reasonably well for monitoring but could be slow when retrieving large data sets. Command-line interfaces were task-oriented and saved commands could be replayed, but their differences made programmatic use difficult. XML was machine-readable and had available tools, but was verbose and lacked commonly accepted management schemas.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop compared six ways to manage devices. Each had strengths, but the report found that no one option met every need.

sections.title: What Network Operators Needed
sections.content:
Operators listed 14 requirements. They asked for easy-to-use tools and a clear separation between configured settings, operational state, and statistics, with a way to retrieve each separately.

They also wanted transactions across multiple devices, configuration backup and restore, comparisons between configurations, and small, low-impact changes. Other requirements covered role-based access control, least privilege, consistent access-control lists, separate configuration distribution from activation, and support for both task-oriented and data-oriented access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators wanted tools that could save, compare, and safely change settings across devices. They also wanted clear access controls and separate views of settings, device state, and statistics.

sections.title: SNMP Findings and Shared Observations
sections.content:
The report lists 20 observations about the SNMP framework. Participants said complete configurations were often unavailable through SNMP, instrumentation quality could be disappointing, large transfers could perform poorly, and management interfaces could be difficult to use for high-level tasks. They also noted that SNMP worked reasonably well for small devices and that eliminating it was not an option.

The consolidated observations call for complete programmatic interfaces, text-based configuration that can be saved and reloaded, secure access control, lower implementation costs, and a way to distinguish configuration from operational data. They also call for both human and programmatic interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants identified limits in using SNMP for complex configuration tasks, while recognizing its value for monitoring. Their broader observations emphasized complete, secure, and easier-to-use management interfaces.

sections.title: Recommendations and Security Note
sections.content:
The workshop made eight recommendations. It called for the IETF to focus resources on standardizing configuration-management mechanisms and for the IETF and IRTF to work on XML-based device configuration and management. It recommended against spending resources on HTML-based or HTTP-based configuration methods.

Other recommendations addressed writable MIB modules, monitoring needs, the SMI and SPPI languages, and the MIB development process. The RFC says that, as a workshop report, it has no direct security implications for the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop's main recommendation was to improve device configuration tools, including work on XML-based approaches. The report itself is a record of a meeting and says it has no direct Internet security implications.
